bio.en: Bob Moesta is co-creator of the Jobs-to-be-Done framework alongside Clay Christensen and founder/CEO of the Rewired Group, helping companies unlock hidden insights to build successful products.
bio.zh: Bob Moesta 是与 Clay Christensen 共同创立“待办任务”（Jobs-to-be-Done）框架的人，也是 Rewired Group 的创始人兼 CEO，帮助企业发掘隐藏洞察以打造成功产品。

summary.en: Bob clarifies a core misconception: Jobs-to-be-Done is about context and outcome, not pain versus gain—the context is what makes seemingly irrational behavior rational. He explains how to interview customers to surface the real struggles behind a switch and when the framework is and isn't a good fit. The conversation includes concrete examples of applying JTBD to both zero-to-one and existing products.
summary.zh: Bob 澄清了一个核心误解：待办任务关注的是“情境与结果”，而非“痛苦与收益”——正是情境让看似非理性的行为变得合理。他解释了如何通过访谈客户来挖掘其转换背后的真实挣扎，以及框架何时适用、何时不适用。对话包含了将 JTBD 应用于从 0 到 1 及既有产品的具体例子。

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: I think one of the biggest misconceptions around Jobs to Be Done is this notion that it's pain and gain as opposed to context and outcome. When you hear somebody's story and it seems irrational, like we'll have people go, "Oh my God, that's an anomaly. That doesn't happen." But what you realize is that the context makes the irrational rational. So the moment you hear a story, you go, "I can't believe that," nine times out of 10, it's because you don't have the rest of the story. And so part of it's being able to understand the rest of that context that would drive somebody to say, "Why would somebody cut their arm off?" Well, if they're in this situation and this and this and this, there's nobody who would say they want to cut their arm off, but in certain situations you'll do it. And so that's what we're trying to do is find, where will people change behavior?
turns.zh: 我认为关于"待完成任务"（Jobs to Be Done）理论，最大的误解之一是人们认为它强调"痛苦与收获"，而非"情境与结果"。当你听到别人的故事时，若觉得不可思议，比如有人会惊呼"天哪，这太反常了，这种事根本不会发生"。但你会发现，只要了解整个情境，许多看似反常的行为就能变得合乎情理。因此，面对这些故事时，人们往往会惊呼"难以置信"，而十有八九是因为他们缺乏完整的背景信息。理解完整的上下文至关重要——这能帮助你理解人们为何会做出看似不可思议的选择。比如，当有人说"为什么有人要切掉自己的手臂？"你可能会感到震惊。但如果他身处特定情境中——比如遭遇某种生存危机或面临极端困境——你就会明白，尽管多数人不会主动选择切断自己的肢体，但在某些特定情境下，人们会被迫做出这种极端选择。我们试图做的，就是找到那些能促使人们改变行为的临界点。

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: I think the easiest way to think about it is that I'm an engineer, electrical, basically have been building product for almost 30 years and one of the lies I was told growing up was build it and they will come. And so we always think about it from a technological, how do I build this thing? And all right, who wants this product? And what I realized very early in my career is that really it didn't work, I couldn't make it work. (00:05:31): And so Jobs to Be Done is this whole premise that people hire products, they don't buy them, they hire them to make progress in their life. And if we can take a step back and look at it, we see it in a very different light to realize at some point they're in some context and there's some outcome they want. And if we can understand that, we start to realize that different things compete, right? (00:05:51): A simple example is think of Snickers and Milky Way, right? They're both candy bars, they're both bought in the checkout aisle, they're both made almost with the same ingredients, one has peanuts, one doesn't. And if you start to compare the products and do a competitive benchmark, you start to get to one's a little softer, one's a little harder, one's got a few more calories, one's got less calories. But when you talk to people about when's the last time they ate a Snickers, when time's the last time they ate a Milky Way, you start to realize that Snickers typically is a case where they missed the last meal, they've got a lot of work to do, they're running out of energy and they want to basically get back to the tasks as fast as possible. And so you start to realize that Snickers is about almost like a meal replacement and it's about the stomach is growling and things like that. And you start to realize that if they didn't have a Snickers, it competes with a protein drink, it competes with a Red Bull, a coffee. (00:06:49): But a Milky Way typically is eaten after an emotional experience, could be positive, could be negative. It's usually eaten alone, and it's taking time to regroup after this emotional thing. And you start to realize that it competes with things like a glass of wine, a brownie, and to be honest, a run. And so when you start to realize that, jobs helps you see the true competitive set from what we call the demand side of the world as opposed to the competitive set from the supply side of the world, which is the technology or the underlying business model by how which we're making it. And so it allows you to actually see what customers really want as opposed to trying to figure out, how do we sell things to people?
turns.zh:
我认为最简单的理解方式是，我是一名工程师，专攻电气领域，过去近30年一直致力于产品开发。但成长过程中有人告诉我一个谎言——“只要你造出产品，用户就会来买”。于是我们总从技术角度出发，思考如何打造产品，却忽视了最根本的问题：用户真正需要什么产品？在职业生涯早期，我意识到这种思路根本行不通——我始终无法让产品成功落地。（00:05:31）  
“工作场景理论”（Jobs to Be Done）提出的核心观点是：用户雇佣产品来推动生活进程，而非简单购买。若我们退后一步审视，就会发现产品存在于特定场景中，并服务于特定目标。理解这一点后，我们会意识到不同产品存在竞争关系。  
（00:05:51）  
举个简单例子：士力架（Snickers）和麦丽素（Milky Way）。两者都是糖果棒，都在超市收银台售卖，成分相似（一个含花生，一个不含）。若从竞争维度分析，两者差异微乎其微：士力架更柔软，热量更高，麦丽素则相反。但当询问用户最近何时吃过士力架或麦丽素时，会发现士力架常出现在人们错过正餐、精力不足、急于恢复状态的场景中；而麦丽素则常出现在情绪波动后需要自我调整的时刻。  
（00:06:49）  
此时，我们会意识到士力架实质上是代餐产品，满足人们在饥饿时的需求；而麦丽素则承载着情感价值，常出现在庆祝或疗愈时刻。  
这启示我们：市场竞争的核心不在于产品本身，而在于满足用户深层需求的场景。传统竞争视角聚焦于技术或商业模式，而Jobs理论则从用户需求出发，帮助我们洞察真实竞争格局，重构市场认知。

turns.speaker: Lenny

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: What's interesting is that at least for me, the thing is what I learned was that supply and demand are not as connected as everybody thinks. Most people think they create a product and that creates demand. But the real thing that if you start to study causality is that a struggling moment causes demand. And you start to realize that in some cases that struggling moment exists and can exist for a long time and nobody solved it. So one of the companies I helped was Southern New Hampshire University and Paul Le Blanc. And one of the things in 2010, we found basically these anomalies, these people who were going to school but not actually coming to class and watching everything online. And it was like 50 or 60 of them and the anomalies basically, and they're paying full price, they didn't want to come. For Paul, it was kind of like why are they doing this? (00:08:29): And when we went to study them, we realized that they actually had a very different job than a typical 18 to 24 year old because one, they were a little bit older, typically they had either already had a degree or they basically had tried to go to college and it didn't work. And it was about basically time now that they had responsibility to do something new. And so they didn't actually build the product at all. And as they started to look and say how many people want to go back to school but can't? They started to realize it's not a thousand people, it's not 10,000 people, they have over 200,000 students. They're one of the largest universities in the world. And so all of this starts with a struggling moment, not with a product. (00:09:06): And so that's what we mean when we're customer-centric is that we're studying the struggling moments they have and people like Intercom and Basecamp, they look at struggling moments and that becomes their roadmap. Because again, think about a roadmap. I'm literally trying to tell you what I'm going to build in the next 24 months, for example, but none of us saw ChatGPT coming. And so all of a sudden I have to go undo the roadmap. But if I talk about the struggling moments that I'm trying to go after, all of a sudden I realize that the roadmap is now when I get to that struggling moment, there's multiple ways I can solve it. So instead of just talking about features, it's typically talking about features for the first 90 to 120 days, but after that we just talk about struggling moments because that's the seed for real innovation and basically where new products come from.
turns.zh: 很有趣的是，至少对我而言，我学到的一点是，供需关系并不像人们想象的那样紧密相连。大多数人认为，他们先创造产品，然后产品就能创造需求。但如果你开始研究因果关系，就会发现，是困境时刻催生了需求。你会逐渐意识到，在某些情况下，这种困境时刻会长期存在却无人解决。我曾帮助的公司之一是南新罕布什尔大学和保罗·勒布朗。2010年，我们发现了一些异常现象——有50到60名学生，他们虽在上学却从不去听课，全程在线学习。他们支付着全额学费，却不愿到校上课。对保罗来说，这就像在问“他们为什么要这样做？”（00:08:29）当我们深入研究后，发现他们与典型的18至24岁年轻人存在巨大差异：首先，他们年龄稍大，通常已有学位，或曾尝试上大学却未成功。此刻，他们肩负着责任去尝试新事物。因此，他们根本没有真正开发产品。当他们开始研究“有多少人想重返校园却无能为力？”时，惊讶地发现这类人群并非千人万人，而是超过20万名学生。他们是全球最大的大学之一。而这一切都始于困境时刻，而非产品本身。（00:09:06）所以，我们所说的以客户为中心，意味着研究客户面临的困境。像Intercom和Basecamp这样的公司，正是通过研究困境时刻来制定路线图的。再想想路线图吧——比如，我现在试图告诉你未来24个月要开发哪些功能，但谁能预见ChatGPT的出现呢？于是我不得不调整路线图。但如果我谈论的是要解决的困境时刻，就会突然意识到，路线图应指向解决困境的时刻。此时，就会涌现出多种解决方案。因此，我们不再只谈论功能特性——前90到120天可能还在谈功能，但之后我们只谈困境时刻，因为这才是真正创新的种子，新产品的源泉。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: To unpack the framework a little bit more, if you were to come to a founder and tell them, "Hey, you should be paying attention to struggling moments," I feel like all of them will say, "Yeah, we know that. We do that. We look for pain and we try to solve it," so what I'm curious there maybe is just what is maybe the right way to do it?
turns.zh: 再深入解析这个框架，如果你对创始人说：“嘿，你应该关注困境时刻。”我觉得他们都会说：“是啊，我们知道这个道理。我们也这么做。我们寻找痛点并试图解决它。”但我好奇的是，或许正确的做法是什么？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: But it's not just the pain. See, what we're taught in business school was pain and gain, but the reality is it's the context. It's the fact that I didn't eat lunch before, the fact that I still have a lot of work to do, the fact that I have this podcast going on. It's not that I'm in pain, but it's the context that makes me value this in the moment that much more than something else. And so part of this is it's not just about pain and gain, it's about context and outcomes. (00:10:34): And so when you frame it that way, it becomes a vector, a vector of progress or a vector of intention of what they're trying to do. And once we frame that, then we can actually wrap technology around it. And the crazy part is that I was always told or taught if I build the best product, it will sell better. And what I've learned is that actually a kick-ass half is better than a half-ass hole, and that's what Jason talks about. But the reality is like if you look at QuickBooks, QuickBooks has half the features and double the price. And you start to realize that at some point in time it's about meeting customers where they are, not trying to wow them and not trying to convince them. They convince themselves to make the progress.
turns.zh:
然而，痛苦并非唯一的因素。你们在商学院学到的是"痛并快乐着"，但现实情况是，关键在于情境。例如，我之前没吃午餐、还有大量工作要做、还要处理播客事务——这些因素并非让我感到痛苦，而是这种情境让我当下比其他事情更珍视眼前这件事。所以这不仅关乎痛苦与收获，更关乎情境与结果。（00:10:34）  
当你以这种方式来理解问题时，它就成了一个向量，一个代表进步的向量，或是代表用户意图的向量。一旦我们明确了这一点，就能围绕它来开发技术了。最令人惊讶的是，我一直被告知或教导：只要做出最好的产品，销量自然会更好。但我发现，有时候半吊子的产品反而比不成熟的方案更受欢迎，杰森（Jason）也提到了这一点。现实情况是，比如QuickBooks，它功能只有一半，但价格却翻倍了。这让你意识到，关键在于满足客户的实际需求，而非试图惊艳他们或说服他们——客户会自己决定如何前进。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'd like to understand this vector piece more because that feels really important. So you were saying that it's not just there's a pain point, solve that, what you're saying is what's even more important is this context around that pain point and things that precede it?
turns.zh: 我想更深入理解这个"向量"的概念，因为这似乎非常重要。你刚刚说，不仅要找到痛点，解决它，更重要的是痛点背后的情境和前置因素？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: Yeah, so the first thing is we don't talk to people who just want to.
turns.zh: 对，首先我们不应该只和那些只想听听就完了的人交流。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: For people listening on the podcast, Bob pulled up a drawing, so you should try to check out the YouTube video of this to see what he's doing.
turns.zh: 对于收听播客的听众，鲍勃展示了一张图示，大家可以去YouTube视频看看他具体怎么操作的。

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: So there's some Product A is the old product and there's some Product B, which is the new product. And ultimately people don't randomly do anything. And so the real heart of the method of Jobs to Be Done is understanding the causation of what pushes people to say, "Today's the day I got to do something different." And the push or the context they're in has nothing to do with the new product, it's the only reason why they would leave the old product. And if there's no push, they can't even see your product because we're creatures of habit, right? And so as soon as I have a push, I call that F1, force one, and I have some idea of what's possible, then I create something called F2, which is basically the pull to a new outcome, a new state, a new thing, right? And so at some point in time it's like I have to be in this situation and I have to want this outcome, right? (00:12:34): But here's the other part is that there's this waterline that there's these other forces and there's two other forces. Every time I show somebody something new, it actually creates anxiety, right? Anxiety of the new, and I call this F3, right? And then the other thing is I have to get them to leave old thing. So I call this habit of the present. And what you start to realize, and I call that F4, is if F1 and F2 are not greater than F3 and F4, they're not going to move, they're not going to do anything. And so ultimately what we're doing is we're framing the market as a system of behavior. And most people say, "If I just add more features, create more pull, people will buy." It's not true. More features create actually anxiety, can it do all those things? (00:13:24): And what you start to realize is if I reduce friction, which is the bottom part, I actually don't have to do anything with a product, I just have to make easier. So for example, one of the things I did is I built houses and one of the frictional points that people had in moving was the fact of moving house was basically packing all their stuff up and going somewhere. And so I would literally sell them a condo, they'd go from a 3000 square foot home to a 1500 square foot condo and they'd cancel six weeks later because they didn't know how to get rid of all their stuff, which is a frictional point. So what did I do? I actually raised the price of the condo, included moving in two years of storage as part of the deal with the condo because it's the frictional coefficient and I increased sales over 30%.
turns.zh: 比如，产品A是旧产品，产品B是新产品。归根结底，人们做任何事情都不是随机的。因此，"待完成任务法"（Jobs to Be Done）的核心在于理解推动人们说出"今天我要尝试新事物"的深层动机。这种推动力或所处的情境与新产品本身无关，它只是促使人们放弃旧产品的唯一原因。如果没有这种推动力，人们甚至都看不到你的产品，因为我们天生就是习惯的产物，对吧？所以，一旦有了推动力，我称之为F1（第一推动力），我就能预见到可能性，然后创造出F2（第二推动力），即对新成果、新状态、新事物的向往，对吧？（00:12:34）但还有另外两个关键因素。每次向别人展示新产品时，都会引发焦虑——对新事物的焦虑，我称之为F3。另外，要让他们愿意放弃旧产品，这需要克服"现状惯性"。当你意识到F1和F2的吸引力若小于F3和F4的阻力时，人们就不会行动。所以归根结底，我们是在把市场视为一个行为系统。大多数人会说："只要增加功能、增强吸引力，人们就会购买。"但这并不正确。过多的功能反而会引发焦虑——它能否实现所有功能？（00:13:24）你会发现，如果减少阻力（即底层因素），就无需过度优化产品，只需让事情更简单。比如，我曾开发住宅项目，人们搬家时面临的阻力之一是打包整理所有物品。所以我直接卖给他们公寓，从3000平方英尺的独户住宅换成1500平方英尺的公寓，但六周后他们就退房了，因为不知道如何处理旧物。这就是阻力所在。于是我提高公寓价格，将两年的仓储服务纳入交易套餐，因为这正是阻力系数所在，最终销售额增长了30%以上。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that.
turns.zh: 我太喜欢这个观点了。

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: So what this is it's really about focusing on the customer. It's about understanding the causation behind it and then using design thinking to actually start to realize, how do we actually enable people to make progress? We don't need to sell them, we need to enable them to buy. (00:14:24): And so I wrote a book called Demand Side Sales that basically took the premise of stop trying to sell people and just help them make progress, help them buy. And so the whole book is instead of trying to base the sales process on how we want to sell, we need to actually design the sales process on how they want to buy. And it seems like it's the same thing, but they're actually really, really different things.
turns.zh: 所以关键在于关注客户，理解背后的因果关系，然后运用设计思维去实现——如何真正帮助人们取得进步？我们不需要向他们推销产品，而是要帮助他们主动购买。（00:14:24）为此我写了一本书《需求侧销售》，核心理念是别再试图向人们推销产品，而是要帮助他们取得进步、实现购买。整本书的核心观点是，销售流程不应基于我们想如何销售，而是要基于客户想如何购买。虽然看似相似，但实则天差地别。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there an example that can make this even more real of a company or a product?
turns.zh: 有没有具体的公司或产品案例能更直观地说明这一点？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: So one of the companies I work with a lot lately is a company called Autobooks, they're based here in Detroit. And basically they help banks basically do invoicing through let's say Apple Pay. And so instead of having to use Square or PayPal, you literally can use your bank now to do these things. And so there's two things, they have to sell small business on it, but they also have to sell banks on it. And when we started talking about it, they talked about why do banks want it? And the first thing we did is we found out there's three really different reasons why banks want them. (00:15:22): But the thing is that where the process looked at is they would talk about the struggling moment, they talk about what was going on and then everything was about getting them to a demo. And once we got them to a demo, we had to close them. Well, it turns out that the buying process literally has different phases in it. There's the first thought, there's something called passive looking where they're problem aware and solution unaware and they have to learn a bunch of things, and then there's active looking where they're both problem and solution aware and they're trying to figure it out and frame a solution, and then there's deciding which is about making trade-offs. (00:15:53): And so what we end up doing is when I started to talk to the team about it, what they started to realize is I said, "Where is the customer in their timeline of buying?" And they looked at me like, "Huh?" I said, "No, no, you have a timeline of how you want to sell to them and after the demo you try to close, but what if they're actually in passive looking and want a demo to learn more? It's very different than if I'm trying to close." And so what we ended up doing is breaking the demo apart, asking people where they were in their buying process. And by doing that we actually then found out a way in which to give them three different demos, one about telling stories and giving them the background about the problem, another one about showing them all the alternatives, and then the last one is about basically giving them choices between ways to move forward, right? (00:16:37): And you'd think that it would make the sales process longer, it actually made the sales process almost half and at 4x basically conversion because now we meet them where they are as opposed to where we want them to be.
turns.zh:
最近我经常合作的一家公司叫Autobooks，总部位于底特律。他们主要帮助银行通过比如Apple Pay等平台进行发票处理。这样一来，客户无需再依赖Square或PayPal等平台，直接使用自己的银行账户即可完成相关操作。  

但要达成这个目标，Autobooks需要同时说服两类客户群体：一是小型企业，二是银行。当我们开始讨论这个项目时，银行方首先提出疑问：为什么银行会需要这样的服务？我们首先发现银行的需求主要源于三个方面：  
（00:15:22）：但现有销售流程存在一个问题——他们总是一味强调“痛点”，而忽视“解决方案”。一旦带客户试用产品，就急于促成交易。但事实上，销售过程分为三个阶段：  
第一阶段是“被动探索期”——客户意识到存在问题，但尚未明确解决方案，需要收集更多信息。  
第二阶段是“主动探索期”——客户既认识到问题，又了解了潜在解决方案，开始尝试构建方案框架。  
第三阶段是“决策期”——客户需要在多个方案中进行权衡，最终做出选择。  
（00:15:53）：因此，我们开始反思：当向团队介绍这个流程时，他们最初的理解是——“客户在购买旅程中的哪个阶段？”但团队成员一脸茫然：“什么？” 我解释道：“你们设定的销售路径是‘试用后促成交易’，但如果客户正处于‘被动探索期’，他们需要先了解问题再考虑解决方案。这和我们常规的促成交易策略完全不同。” 

最终，我们将试用流程拆分成三个阶段，根据客户所处阶段提供对应的演示内容：  
第一阶段：“讲述故事”——介绍问题背景  
第二阶段：“展示方案”——列举所有替代方案  
第三阶段：“提供选择”——引导客户选择推进方向  
（00:16:37）：看似流程变长，但实际转化率提升了4倍，因为我们顺应了客户的实际需求，而非强行套用标准路径。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And is that something you find generally in the sales process, there's these three phases that everyone goes through and you got to think about them individually?
turns.zh: 在销售过程中，大家普遍会经历这三个阶段吗？需要针对每个阶段分别制定策略吗？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: Yeah, there's actually, I call them six phases. First thought, passive looking, active looking, deciding, first use, and then ongoing use. How do we build the new habit? And so if we don't actually study that part of how do people transform themselves through a struggling moment, we don't know what they want. If I talk to people who want to buy a house, they tell me they want granite and hardwood and they'll make everything these things they want. (00:17:25): But when you actually talk to people who bought a house, they actually made a lot of trade-offs. Although for example, everybody I would survey before buying a house, I had 93% say they wanted an Energy Star compliant house. It cost 30 grand to make an Energy Star compliant at the time. And the reality is nobody bought it, they all bought the finished basement. And so there's the difference between what they say they want and what they want. (00:17:48): And so the method itself is not based on traditional research or market research, asking people what it is. It's actually based on criminal and intelligence interrogation about telling me the story about how you decided today's the day I bought a house or today's the day I went back to school. It's not random. And if it's not random, then we need to actually find it. And that to me is one of the bigger differences, most people build their sales process on probability, "If I get so many leads in, I'll convert so many to here to so many..." But the ultimate thing is, how many people are really ready for your product? They have to actually be ready for it. And that's what Jobs to Be Done is really about, is understanding where they are, what's causing it, and how do they make the trade-offs?
turns.zh: 是的，实际上，我把这个过程分为六个阶段。第一阶段是初步想法，第二阶段是被动观察，第三阶段是主动探索，第四阶段是做出决定，第五阶段是首次使用，第六阶段是持续使用。我们如何养成新习惯呢？如果我们不深入研究人们如何在困境中改变自己的行为模式，我们就无法真正理解他们的需求。比如，我和想买房的人交谈时，他们告诉我他们想要花岗岩和硬木地板，还会把所有东西都改造成他们想要的样子。（00:17:25）但当你真正和买过房的人交流时，他们其实做了很多妥协。例如，我在买房前调查的人中，93%说他们想要符合能源之星标准的房子。当时达到这个标准要花3万美元，但现实情况是没人买这种房子，大家都买了带装修的地下室。这就是人们嘴上说和实际想要之间的差距。（00:17:48）所以这个方法本身不是基于传统的市场调研或问卷调查，而是基于刑侦和情报审讯的思路，去倾听他们讲述自己是如何决定买房或重返校园的。这不是随机的。既然不是随机的，那我们就必须去挖掘其中的规律。在我看来，这就是最大的区别之一。大多数人构建销售流程都是基于概率思维：“如果我获取了这么多潜在客户，就能转化多少到下一步……”。但关键问题是，真正准备好购买你产品的人有多少？他们必须真的有需求。这才是“工作完成理论”（Jobs to Be Done）真正要解决的问题——理解他们的现状、背后的驱动因素，以及他们如何权衡利弊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So let's follow that thread of interviewing and talking to your potential customers and customers to understand the jobs to be done. What is the actual process you recommend?
turns.zh: 那么，接下来我们要按照这个思路去采访和沟通潜在客户和现有客户，以了解他们需要完成的工作。你具体推荐的流程是怎样的？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: The first thing we do is we frame a question. And the way I think about it is most people, so the one thing to know about me is I've been building things for over 30 years, I've worked on 3,500 different products and services across many, many industries, but I've had three close head brain injuries before I was seven years old and I can't read and I can't write. And so one of the things for me is that I could not understand the research that I would get from marketing around basically they'd say, "Hey, I need something that's easy, fast and fun and cheap." And I'd be like, "Okay, what does any of that mean? What is fast? How fast is fast and what's not fast?" And you start to undo all those things. (00:19:18): And so the first thing we do is we start to frame, let's just talk about what causes people to say today's the day they want to go on vacation or today's the day they wanted a new set of windows. And you start to frame around that, and then you go find people who recently purchased and say, "What in the world happened that says today's the day I need new windows?" And you start to realize that there's pushes and there's pulls and there's anxieties and there's habits. And so the first thing we do is we try to extract the story from the customer. And it doesn't have to be my product, it could be somebody else's product if I haven't built it yet. It's like, what are people going to fire when they hire me? (00:19:55): And so when we get the stories though, then the stories are going to get us the pushes, the pulls, the anxieties and the habits, the trade-offs and what we call the hire and fire criteria. And then what we do is instead of trying to look for themes across all of them, we actually do something, instead of segmenting them, we cluster them, we find the pathways because what you start to realize is it's not one reason why people do it, it's sets of reasons. And those sets actually work together. So the pushes work with the pulls. So when they have these pushes, they want these pulls. And when they don't have these pushes, they don't want those pulls. (00:20:29): And so when you start to see the patterns and you start to pull it out, you start to realize that most companies or most products are hired to do 3, 4, 5 different jobs and they're in conflict with each other. One person wants to go faster and one person wants to be more thorough. And so all of a sudden being more thorough means it's slower. If I say we're thorough, the people who want it fast say, "I don't want this because it's too slow." So how do you frame those things out and understand where the conflicts are behind it and think about different products from it? (00:20:59): That's what Intercom did, right? Intercom realized that people hired it for four very, very different reasons and then instead of building four different products, they literally took their product and turned off the features that were not relevant to the pathway that people wanted to take. So for acquire, they didn't need a whole bunch of these other features and so they actually framed it around basically, how do we help people convert? And that job actually competed with HubSpot. (00:21:24): There's another one where it was about helping with support, and that one competed with Zendesk. And so they changed the pricing model to basically match who the competition was and to match the progress that people were trying to make because Zendesk was too much and too hard, and HubSpot felt like it was an overkill for where people were. We basically figured out how to actually position ourselves as a good next step between HubSpot adds nothing or between nothing and HubSpot. And that's how they've grown to be valued over 2 billion.
turns.zh:
我们的首要任务是明确问题所在。就我个人而言，我在30多年来一直致力于产品开发，参与过众多行业的3500款产品和服务项目。但在七岁前，我曾遭遇三次严重的头部创伤，导致我至今无法阅读和书写。因此，当我面对市场调研报告时，比如“我们需要简单、快捷、趣味且低成本的产品”之类需求时，总会疑惑：“这些词汇到底意味着什么？‘快’有多快？什么才算不快？” 于是我不得不从头拆解这些概念。（00:19:18）首先，我们要深入理解用户行为背后的深层动机。比如，人们为何会说“今天是度假的绝佳时机”或“今天我需要换新窗户”？通过深度访谈，我们能发现这些决策背后存在着推动力与阻力因素、焦虑情绪与习惯偏好，以及权衡取舍的考量。最终，我们需要从用户视角提炼核心故事——即便产品尚未成型，这也能帮助我们预判用户的真实需求。

（00:19:55）通过故事洞察，我们能精准捕捉用户的痛点与驱动力。这些故事不仅揭示了产品卖点，还暴露了潜在的冲突点。比如，用户可能希望产品既快捷又全面，但实际需求却相互矛盾。例如，追求速度的用户与追求全面的用户存在天然冲突——前者需要高效，后者则要求严谨。因此，产品定位需聚焦核心场景，整合相关功能，避免功能冗余。

（00:20:29）Intercom的成功案例值得借鉴。该公司发现用户需求可分为四大类：获取客户、支持服务、定价策略及协作工具。针对不同场景，Intercom选择关闭非核心功能，专注核心任务。例如，针对获取客户的场景，他们简化了产品逻辑，专注于转化率优化；而针对支持服务的场景，则与Zendesk形成差异化竞争。通过动态调整定价策略，他们成功切入了竞争空白区，满足了用户的实际需求。

（00:21:24）类似案例还有HubSpot与Zendesk的差异化竞争。HubSpot专注于客户转化，Zendesk则专注于客户支持。Intercom通过定价策略实现了与竞品的精准对标，既匹配了Zendesk的复杂性，又满足了HubSpot的过度功能。最终，Intercom通过精准定位，成功构建了产品护城河。
他们将自己定位为HubSpot与其他工具之间的一个优质过渡选择，或者说是在无任何工具与HubSpot之间架起桥梁。正因如此，他们的估值已突破20亿美元大关。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I have a follow-up question, but did you say that you can't read and write?
turns.zh: 我还有一个后续问题，但你刚说你不识字也不识字？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: Yeah, can't read and write. So the thing is I cannot read the words that I write and I cannot read... So if somebody reads it to me, I can actually play it back. So I'll listen to audio. But the fact is the way I was taught to read is so that when I look at a paragraph, I see the spaces between the words first, and then I usually see the left-hand edge of the words, so the last three letters. And so my mom taught me to look at the five largest words on the page by circling the longest words on the page. And then I would study those and translate those and then figure out what those five words would have in common. Because for me, the part that's broken in my brain is that I can't look up things fast enough. So by the time I try to look at a word, figure out what it is, get the definition, I've literally forgotten every word before it.
turns.zh: 是的，我不识字也不识字。所以问题在于，我无法读懂自己写的字，也无法读懂别人写的字……如果别人读给我听，我倒是能复述出来。所以我会听音频。但事实是，我学到的阅读方法是，当我看一段文字时，首先看到的是字与字之间的空格，然后通常能看到单词的左边缘，也就是最后三个字母。我妈妈教我先圈出页面上最长的单词，再研究这些单词并翻译它们，然后找出这五个单词的共同点。因为对我来说，大脑中出了问题的地方在于，我无法快速查找信息。所以当我试图看一个字、弄清楚它是什么、查找定义时，前面的字早已经忘了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Damn. How are you writing books?
turns.zh: 天哪。你怎么能写书呢？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: It's a gift. I'm telling you, it's a gift. It's a gift I'd never wish upon my children. But to be honest, it's given me abilities to see patterns in so many different ways because I can remember the first five words in the first paragraph and the last five words in the last paragraph so I turned through a book three or four times, and I have as good a comprehension as everybody else.
turns.zh: 这是一种天赋。我跟你说，这是天赋。我绝不会希望自己的孩子拥有这种天赋。但说实话，它让我能以多种方式发现规律，因为我能记住第一段的前五个单词和最后一段的后五个单词，所以我会把一本书通读三四遍，理解能力和其他人一样好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is insane. How are you writing books?
turns.zh: 这太不可思议了。你怎么能写书呢？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: It's really simple, I have a company called Scribe Media, and what we do is first thing we do is we look for what struggling moments do people have? We then look at what are the competitive books wrapped around it? I then basically outline what progress looks like. We then take each chapter and define it as a system and what we have to do in each chapter to help them make the progress along the way. And then we just talk and we talk, we have ten two hour sessions, they get recorded, and then somebody basically takes... So if you listen or read any of my books, it sounds like me talking because it is.
turns.zh: 其实很简单，我有一家叫Scribe Media的公司。我们首先会研究人们在学习过程中遇到的困难，然后看看围绕这些困难的竞品书籍是什么。接着我会勾勒出进步的路径。我们把每章内容定义为一个系统，明确每章需要做什么来帮助读者取得进展。然后我们会不断沟通，进行十次两小时的会谈，这些会谈会被录音，之后有人会整理……所以如果你听或读我的书，听起来就像我在说话，因为确实如此。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow.
turns.zh: 哇。

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: And so I can get a book out in three and a half, four months.
turns.zh: 所以我能在三个月半、四个月内完成一本书。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's incredible.
turns.zh: 太不可思议了。

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: And so now I'm a teacher, I'm adjunct lecturer at the Kellogg School at Northwestern, and then I guest lecture on the East Coast in kind of different business schools, and then I help Techstars and Y Combinator. So I'm really moving myself into being into, I feel it's time to pass on. I've had some amazing mentors who helped me, and again, I was told to be a baggage handler or a construction worker when I graduated high school, and my mom thought I could do more. And so I met these people who poured their knowledge into me to enable me to do all this stuff so now I'm trying to pay it forward as much as I can. So that's one of the reasons why I do as many podcasts as I can. So again, I appreciate you having me.
turns.zh: 现在我是一名教师，在西北大学凯洛格商学院担任兼职讲师，还在东海岸的不同商学院做客座讲座，同时为Techstars和Y Combinator提供帮助。所以我真的在努力将知识传递下去，我觉得是时候把火炬传递下去了。高中毕业时，人们建议我去当行李搬运工或建筑工人，但我妈妈认为我能做得更多。然后我遇到了那些向我传授知识的人，让我能做成现在这些事，所以现在我尽可能多地做播客回馈社会。所以再次感谢你们邀请我。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, this is a great opportunity to pass it on and so I'm very happy we're doing that. I had no idea about any of this about you, so thank you for sharing that.
turns.zh: 是的，这是一个很好的传递知识的机会，所以我很高兴我们能这样做。我对你的情况一无所知，所以谢谢你分享这些。

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: It's been fun. I pinched myself. The other part is I don't know how I got here. One of the things that I've been doing is I've been studying people for the last 10 years around why they switched from one company to another to literally understand the jobs of jobs because employees actually hire companies more than companies hire employees. And so you start to realize the struggling moment is why don't we have enough people? And otherwise I want to leave, but I don't know how to leave. And so I'm in the midst of writing a book around that right now with Michael Horn and Ethan Bernstein.
turns.zh: 这一切都很有趣。我掐了自己一下。另一方面，我不知道自己怎么会走到今天这一步。过去十年间，我一直在研究人们从一家公司跳槽到另一家公司的原因，试图真正理解工作的本质——因为实际上是员工在选择公司，而非公司在选择员工。于是你会意识到，职场困境往往在于“我们为什么招不到足够的人才？”而另一些人则想离开，却又不知如何迈出这一步。目前我正与迈克尔·霍恩（Michael Horn）和伊桑·伯恩斯坦（Ethan Bernstein）合作撰写一本相关书籍。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there an insight from that work that you can share about why people leave jobs or join jobs?
turns.zh: 从这项研究中，你能否分享一些关于人们离职或入职的深刻见解？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: So the number one thing that I would say is almost everybody when you ask them about how they got the job they're in, the number one phrase you get is, "It was so lucky. I was so lucky, just happened to fall in my lap." And then when you actually unpack the story, luck had nothing to do with it. They were prepped, they were ready, there was pushes, there were pulls, there was anxieties, they were able to do it. And you start to realize, and the funny part is that if I talked to somebody who's been through three or four kind of switches, they all can say, "Yep, I've had that job. Yep, I've had that job. Yep, I've had that." And so there's frames around basically understanding what progress are you really trying to make now? Is it, do I need balance? Am I not challenged enough? (00:26:08): And you start to frame it, and when you frame it, you start to realize, I'm willing to actually take less money to be around smarter people because I want to be a founder later. And so you start to realize that all of these things where we think we have to pay more money, over 50% of the people who got new jobs didn't get more money. It's a lie. It's about progress. It's about what do they want to learn? What skills do they want to get? At some point it's about money, but it's not always about money. (00:26:37): And the other interesting part is when you talk about money, we talk about this notion of unpacking. We'll say, "Well, why do you need more money?" It's like, "Well, I have larger obligations," or, "I want more money because I want more respect." And so what you realize is in the hiring and firing criteria, they talk about money, but money actually has a bigger effect than just money. It's about respect or it's about responsibility or it's about their metric of progress. There's a whole bunch of things, but it's not just money. That's the interesting part.
turns.zh: 我要说的首要观点是，几乎所有人当被问及如何获得现有职位时，最常说的是“真是太幸运了。运气太好了”，仿佛一切都是偶然。但当你深入剖析这个故事时，就会发现运气其实与此无关。他们经过了充分准备，克服了重重阻碍，承受了焦虑，最终成功上岸。有趣的是，那些经历过三四次跳槽的人都会感慨：“没错，我曾做过那份工作，没错，我也经历过那份工作，没错，我也遇到过那样的情况。”这揭示了一个核心问题：我们现在真正追求的是什么？是平衡？还是挑战不足？（00:26:08）当你重新审视这些问题时，你会意识到，我愿意为了更聪明的人而降低薪资，因为我未来想成为创始人。由此可见，绝大多数跳槽者并未获得更高的薪资。这是个谎言。关键在于个人成长——在于他们想学习什么技能，获取何种能力。在某些时候，薪资固然重要，但并非唯一考量因素。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I've definitely done that myself, there's a status component to your job.
turns.zh: 是的，我自己也曾这样做过，工作确实带有身份认同的成分。

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: Yeah, I want the title, right? Happens all the time.
turns.zh: 没错，我也渴望那个头衔，对吧？这种情况屡见不鲜。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to come back to the discussion we were just having around interviewing people to understand the jobs to be done. And a bunch of people on LinkedIn were trying to understand just tactically what they need to get right in order to get accurate jobs. So I guess, are there just a couple tactics you'd recommend for how to interview people?
turns.zh: 我想回归到我们刚刚讨论的通过访谈理解待办工作的议题。LinkedIn上许多人都在探讨如何通过实际方法准确把握工作需求。所以我想问，你能否分享一些访谈技巧？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: Let me give you three tips. The first tip I'd tell you is go read Never Split The Difference by Chris Voss. I started to write a book around basically techniques that I learned back in the eighties and nineties around this, and his book is amazing around it, the whole notion of getting to know. I play things back incorrectly because they're going to say no, and I'm going to say, "All right, fix it," and then they'll talk more. The moment somebody says yes, there's nothing more to say. And so there's a bunch of techniques you have to learn to basically get them talking. (00:28:09): The second is I only talk to people who have already tried to make the progress, right? So for example, people talk about like, "Well, you can't apply this to something that's new. It doesn't exist." So I worked with a company that was, let's say a fairly large social media company, and at some point in time they found people kind of transacting on their platform, but they didn't know anything about it and they hadn't built anything. And what they ended up doing is we ended up going and studying eBay and Etsy and what caused somebody to say, "Today's the day I'm going to set up an eBay store or sell something on Craigslist." And out of that, we found all the jobs of what people, both sellers were doing and buyers were doing, and now I think it's I think almost a $3 billion marketplace that didn't exist and they learned about it all from the competitors.
turns.zh: 让我给你们三个建议。第一个建议是去读克里斯·沃斯（Chris Voss）的《永不妥协的谈判艺术》（Never Split The Difference）。我在八九十年代就开始研究这些谈判技巧，而他的书在这方面堪称杰作，核心在于如何建立信任。我过去常常错误地解读对方的反应，因为他们会说“不行”，然后我会说“好的，那就改改吧”，接着他们就会说更多话。而一旦对方说“好吧”，那就没什么可说的了。所以你必须掌握一系列技巧，才能让他们开口畅谈。（00:28:09）第二个建议是，只和已经取得进展的人交流。举个例子，人们可能会说：“你不能把这个应用到新事物上，因为它根本不存在。” 我曾与一家相当大的社交媒体公司合作，他们发现有人在平台上进行交易，但自己对此一无所知，也没有开发相关功能。最后，我们研究了eBay和Etsy，了解是什么促使人们说“今天我要在eBay开店或者在Craigslist上卖东西”。通过这些研究，我们发现了卖家和买家正在做的一系列行为。如今，这个市场规模接近30亿美元，而之前根本不存在，所有信息都是从竞争对手那里学来的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Sounds like Facebook Marketplace, maybe? No comment?
turns.zh: 听起来像Facebook Marketplace，对吧？不予置评？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: I didn't say that.
turns.zh: 我可没这么说。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How many interviews do you recommend people do to get to a confident?
turns.zh: 你建议人们进行多少次访谈才能变得自信？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: That's a great controversial question. The interesting part is from a causal mechanism perspective and from a set theory perspective, meaning the sets of pushes, pulls anxieties and habits, it starts to repeat around seven or eight. And I usually do 10, no more than 12. And I would rather do two rounds of 12 interviews than do 24 interviews. I had some really interesting mentors, one of them was Dr. Deming, who's the father of lean and quality systems and like that. And so he would always push me to basically how to do things faster and smaller. And so that's where a lot of it came. And you just realize that people will say, "Oh, we have to do something statistically significant." Well, you do if you're doing it randomly, but if you actually understand the range of your market and you know that 50% of it is above 30 years old and 50% is below 30 years old, I could actually sample in a way that makes me get a good representation without having to actually do 50 interviews. And so we use something called design experiments to help with that.
turns.zh: 这是个很有争议的好问题。从因果机制和集合论的角度看，推动和拉动因素、焦虑和习惯的集合，大约在七到八次时开始重复。我通常做10次访谈，不超过12次。我宁愿分两轮各做12次访谈，也不愿做24次访谈。我有一些非常出色的导师，其中一位是戴明博士，他是精益和质量体系之父。他总是督促我如何更快、更高效地做事。很多想法都源于此。你会发现人们会说：“哦，我们必须做具有统计学意义的研究。” 如果你随机抽样当然可以，但如果你了解市场范围，知道50%的人年龄在30岁以上，50%在30岁以下，我就能通过抽样获得准确的代表性，而无需做50次访谈。我们使用设计实验来实现这一目标。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love the concrete numbers. And so along those lines, when you're actually asking questions of people, do you have any best practices and ways of phrasing a question to get a response you can trust?
turns.zh: 我喜欢具体的数据。基于此，当你真正向人们提问时，有没有什么最佳实践和提问方式能获得可靠的回应？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: In a lot of cases, you have to look at it from multiple perspectives. And so the other tip I have is to not have a discussion guide. It drives people crazy because everybody wants to ask the same set of questions, but the problem happens is when you ask the same set of questions, you actually don't follow the ones that actually have the most meaningful information in it, right? And so what happens is, what I say is I use the framework of pushes, pulls, anxieties and habits and say, "What caused them to do this?" And everything else is just a conversation of trying to understand their story. (00:30:53): And so part of this is being able to ask the questions around why, but you can't ask "Why, why, why, why why?" It's like, "Tell me more about that. Give me an example." And in a lot of cases, I usually get them to what I call the edge of language where they have no more language, and what I do is I literally then bracket it, "So was it more about this or more about that?" And I know it's neither one of those, and it forces them to talk more, right? It's always trying to get them to know, because the moment I get to... So when I play it back, "So you did this and this and this and this," and say, "No, that wasn't it." And the people who I'm working with are like, "You know that's not the right answer," I'm like, "I know, but they're going to elaborate on why it's not that." And so it's literally being able to reveal kind of the causal mechanisms of why people do what they do.
turns.zh: 很多时候，你需要从多个角度去看待问题。还有一个建议是，别用讨论指南。这会让人抓狂，因为每个人都想问同一套问题，但问题在于，当你问同样的问题时，往往会忽略那些真正有价值的信息，对吧？所以我的做法是，使用"推动力、拉动力、焦虑感和习惯"这个框架，问"是什么促使他们这样做的？"然后其他的讨论都是试图理解他们的故事。（00:30:53）：所以关键在于能够提出为什么的问题，但你不能一直追问"为什么，为什么，为什么，为什么为什么？"而是应该说，"再给我讲讲。举个例子吧。"很多时候，我通常会把他们带到语言的边缘地带——他们已经无话可说了。这时我就会用括号框住问题："所以这更多是关于这个还是那个？"我知道答案不在其中任何一个选项里，这样就能迫使他们继续深入解释。每次我回放录音时，比如"你做了这个、这个、这个、这个"，他们会说"不，不是这样的"。我同事会说"你知道这不是正确答案"，我回应"我知道，但他们会解释为什么不是"。最终就是要揭示人们行为背后的因果机制。
