turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: So what I would say is I find a lot of founders, especially really successful founders, like I would say Jason Fried is one of those where he intuitively understood this. He actually thinks this way but didn't have language wrapped around it, right? So I think that it's a very useful framework. I think that the danger you run into is that when you look at the customer through the product, so if I look at the customers through the Snickers bar, then I think of Milky Way as a competitor. But if I look at the customer and say, "Why did they pick that thing?" Then I realize that a protein shake and an apple and a sandwich are the competitors not Milky Way.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，我发现很多创业者——尤其是那些非常成功的创业者——比如杰森·弗里德（Jason Fried），他就很能领悟这一点。他实际上是这么想的，但当时并没有用语言把这种想法表达出来。对此我认为这是一个非常有用的框架。但你可能会遇到的危险是，当你从产品角度看待客户时，比如如果我通过士力架（Snickers bar）来看待客户，那么我会把银河巧克力（Milky Way）视为竞争对手。但如果你从客户的角度出发，问“他们为什么会选择那个产品？”你就会意识到，蛋白质奶昔、苹果和三明治才是真正的竞争对手，而不是银河巧克力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. So say someone wanted to start going in this direction of Jobs to Be Done, what is the simplest, I don't know, first version, lightweight approach to starting to think this way?
turns.zh: 明白了。那么如果有人想开始朝着“工作完成”（Jobs to Be Done）的方向发展，最简单、最基础、最轻量级的入门方法是什么？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: So there's two things. If I have a product, go find 10 people who recently bought your product, but what I want you do is go talk to them, not about the product, but about why they bought the product, what was going on, what were they hoping for, what were they worried about? What did they have to give up? How did they convince somebody else? Just listen to the story. Start with just getting the story. (00:34:26): Because there's three levels of information we have to get or three sources of energy that I talk about. So think about it as there's got to be energy in the system for us to do something. And there's what I call functional energy, which is usually time, space, effort, knowledge, right? There's emotional energy, which is how I feel. I want to feel better, I feel frustrated, I feel overlooked. There's emotional aspects to it. And then there's social aspects, how I want others to perceive me or how others perceive me, "Oh, my boss is going to fire me because he doesn't think I'm doing this fast enough and I feel inadequate." So part of his understanding kind of the emotional, social and functional components that are part of that energy source.
turns.zh: 有两个方面。如果我有一款产品，先去找10个最近购买过你产品的用户，但我希望你做的不是和他们谈论产品本身，而是去探讨他们为什么购买这款产品，他们当时面临怎样的情况，他们的期望是什么，他们又在担忧什么，他们不得不放弃什么，他们是如何说服他人的。只要倾听他们的故事就行了。先从获取故事入手。（00:34:26）：因为我们要做某件事，就必须获得三种信息，或者说三种能量来源。我把这看作是系统中必须存在的能量。其中有功能性能量，通常包括时间、空间、努力、知识等；情绪能量，比如我的感受，我想感觉更好，我感到沮丧，我觉得被忽视了；还有社会性能量，即我希望他人如何看待我，或者他人如何看待我，“哦，我的老板要解雇我了，因为他觉得我做得不够快，我觉得自己不够格。”所以理解情绪、社会和功能性这些能量成分是关键。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it.
turns.zh: 明白了。

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: The second part is if it's an established product and it's been there a while, I'd actually go and talk to people who churned. Because in churn, what's interesting is when somebody leaves your product, they're still making progress. We think it's bad for us, which it probably is, but in their mind it's like, "Yeah, this was too hard and complicated," or, "You know what? It didn't do enough for us." It allows you to actually understand the struggling moment they had because, again, they were using your product and something happened and some context changed and now they struggle with it, and now they got to go find something else. (00:35:43): Nobody wants to change. So that makes this actually the easiest thing to look at is tell me why people change. We just seem to literally not want to go deep enough and we use the lazy word of random and probability as pseudo for knowledge, and it's not knowledge. It's literally just if context is the same, if outcomes is the same, then I can do it. But if I listen to football stats, third down in preseason is very different than third down in playoffs, right? And so giving me a stat about how their third down conversion is across the whole season makes no sense to me because the context is different.
turns.zh: 第二部分是，如果这是一款已有的产品，并且已经存在一段时间了，我会去和那些流失用户交流。因为流失用户很有意思的是，当他们离开你的产品时，他们其实还在不断进步。我们觉得这对我们不利，可能确实如此，但在他们看来，他们会说：“是啊，这个太难太复杂了。”或者，“你知道吗？它对我们帮助不够。”这能让你真正理解他们在挣扎的时刻，因为他们之前一直在使用你的产品，后来情况发生了变化，现在他们陷入困境，不得不另觅他处了。（00:35:43）：没有人愿意改变。所以这其实是最容易入手的切入点——告诉我人们为什么会改变。我们似乎总是不愿深入探究，而是用概率和随机性之类的词来替代知识，但这根本不是知识。如果环境相同，结果相同，那我就能做到。但如果我听足球数据，季前赛的三档进攻和季后赛的三档进攻是完全不同的，对吧？所以给我整个赛季三档进攻成功率的数据毫无意义，因为环境不同了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You brought up this point that people often say they really hate something and it comes across that they're ready to switch and will use something that you've built that's better, but they don't because of that friction you mentioned. What do you look for that might tell you that they're really actually going to use it for real and it's that serious?
turns.zh: 你提到了一个观点：人们常说自己非常讨厌某样东西，听起来他们准备换用你开发的更优质产品，但最终却因为你提到的摩擦因素而未能行动。你是如何判断他们是否真的会去真正使用它、并且态度足够认真呢？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: The very first thing I would say is I never trust anybody telling me things they're going to do because they can't assure it, and it usually never happens. It's my experience that says that. And so the thing is, I need to talk to people who did something and tried and though they might've failed, what made them try? So the phrase I have 'Bitchin' ain't switchin'." Just because people bitch about something doesn't mean they're going to do anything about it. This is where at Basecamp, we learned the fact that everybody said, "Oh, if you had Gantt charts, I'm going to leave you if you don't put Gantt charts in or resource allocation," and as much as they all say they want it, they're not leaving because of it. (00:37:23): And this is the other part, if you follow your best users, they'll take you up to this world that then actually destroys the lower end of the world of why people are there. And so if Basecamp would've added all those things, one of the reasons why people join Basecamp is because it's so dang simple. And if I start to add all these things that make it more complicated, it doesn't work.
turns.zh: 首先，我要说的是，我从不相信那些声称要做某事的人，因为他们往往无法兑现承诺。根据我的经验，这种情况屡见不鲜。所以关键在于，我需要和那些尝试过却失败的人交流，探究他们为何愿意尝试。正如我常说的那样：“吐槽归吐槽，行动归行动。”仅仅因为人们抱怨某样东西，并不意味着他们会采取行动。在Basecamp，我们就遇到过这样的情况：用户纷纷要求添加甘特图、资源分配等功能，但尽管他们口口声声说想要这些功能，最终却没有因此离开平台。（00:37:23）另一方面，若你紧随最忠实的用户，他们会带你进入一个全新的世界，但这往往会毁掉那些低端用户的使用体验。比如，如果Basecamp添加了所有这些复杂功能，吸引新用户的核心优势——极致的简洁性就会消失。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And so in those conversations, is there something you find that just this is a sign they're actually really serious, or do you just like, "I'm not going to listen to anything they're saying in this case until we actually build it and they're using it"?
turns.zh: 在这些交流中，有没有什么迹象能表明他们是认真的，还是说你会选择：“在产品真正上线并投入使用之前，我不会听信他们的任何承诺。”

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: So for example, in the first five minutes of an interview, they're going to tell you, "I bought a new car because I got a deal on it and it was a car I've been dreaming about forever," and it's like they have all these things and then when you start to get to, it's like, no, the old car had 280,000 miles on it. You had three large bills in the last four months. The fact is it's making a sound and you've got a long trip coming up, that's why you're getting a car. You're not getting the car because of the deal. And so there's these, I call it the layers of language. And the very first layer is called the pablum layer, where people just, "How was your day?" "Oh, it was good," but nobody knows what that means. And if you ask one further question, "Well, what was good about it?" They're like, "Ugh." (00:38:34): And then you get to the next layer, the next layer is usually the fantasy nightmare layer, "Oh, it was so good because of this," or, "Oh my God, it was so bad because..." They exaggerate to one degree or the next. And then what you want to do is actually then pull it back to what actually happened. This is where you've got to be more of an investigator and an interrogator. And the way I would describe it is it's criminal and intelligence interrogation that feels like therapy because most people don't actually know why they bought because they only think about the time they wrote the check, swiped the card. But the reality is like I did an interview with somebody who bought a coat rack, $137 coat rack. It took them 18 months to buy it. And in their mind, they say they bought it in a week, but the reality is the debate about getting it and why they couldn't get it was happening for over 18 months. So this is where you can't believe what they say, you have to do your investigation to get there.
turns.zh:
举个例子，在面试的前五分钟，他们会告诉你：“我买了一辆新车，因为价格很划算，而且这是我梦寐以求的车。” 但当你深入探讨时，就会发现事实并非如此。比如旧车已经行驶了28万英里，过去四个月里他们有三笔大额账单。更关键的是，车子现在有噪音问题，而他们马上要进行长途旅行，所以才决定换车。买车并非因为优惠价格。  

我把这种现象称为“语言分层”。最初的分层叫“糊涂层”，比如“今天过得怎么样？”“挺好的。”但没人真正明白这句话的含义。再追问一句：“有什么好的地方？”对方就会回答：“哎呀。”  

接下来是幻想噩梦层：“太棒了，因为……”、“天哪，太糟糕了，因为……”。他们会夸大其词或添油加醋。你的任务是把话题拉回现实，充当调查者和审讯者。这种方法有点像刑事审讯和情报审讯，只不过更像心理治疗，因为大多数人其实不清楚自己购买的真正原因——他们只记得写支票或刷卡的那一刻。  

比如我采访过一个买衣架的人，他花了18个月才买下一个137美元的衣架。在他自己看来，只用了一周时间，但实际上，关于是否购买以及为何未能购买的讨论持续了18个月以上。  

所以别轻信他们的话，要通过调查才能了解真相。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And what does that phrase use again for that vector of progress?
turns.zh: 那句话用来描述进展的维度是什么？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: The intention, it's the context that they're in and the outcome. So here's the thing is that most people talk about you want to get to this outcome and people value this outcome, but value is not just the outcome. Value also has where you start. So if I start here and I end here, I'm going to value it this much. But if I start down here... Wait, I've got to get there, start down here, and I go up here, I value it that much more. And so part of it is value is actually part of where they're starting from and where they want to go. And most people say, "If I just get them up here, they're really going to love it," but some people say, "I just want to get here." And so you're overshooting it and they actually want a price discount because you're giving them more than they want.
turns.zh:
意图、背景和结果。比如大多数人只关注结果，但价值不仅仅是结果，还包括起点和终点。如果起点低，终点高，价值自然更高。但如果起点高，终点低，价值同样很高。所以价值不仅关乎结果，还关乎起点和终点。  

大多数人会说：“只要能达到这个结果，他们就会喜欢。”但有些人说：“我只想达到结果。” 你可能用力过猛，而他们真正想要的是折扣，因为你给他们的超出预期。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So I'm going to go in a different direction. The most liked comment on LinkedIn asking people what question to ask you was by Sharam Krishnan, who's actually on this podcast in the past.
turns.zh: 那我换个方向。LinkedIn上最受欢迎的提问是Sharam Krishnan提出的，他以前参加过我们的播客。

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: Yeah, yeah, yeah. I remember seeing it, I remember hearing it. By the way, I think it's one of the reasons why I reached out because I'm like, "Okay, we need to clarify this a little."
turns.zh: 是的，是的。我记得看到过，也记得听过这个问题。顺便说一句，我觉得这也是我联系他的原因之一，因为我觉得：“好吧，我们需要把这事理清楚一点。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, great. So you saw the brand, he's not what you'd say a fan of Jobs to Be Done.
turns.zh: 好的，很棒。看来你注意到品牌了，他可不是“工作要做”理论的粉丝。

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: No, no.
turns.zh: 不，不。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And so here's the question he wanted to ask, "Is there a case of a startup or a modern technology company or any company that was using Jobs to Be Done to launch a product from zero to one that has had broad adoption?" That's his challenge.
turns.zh: 以下是原文的翻译：

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: Inside the company or broad adoption that the product that we've developed had broad adoption?
turns.zh: 接下来是他想问的问题：“有没有初创公司、现代科技公司或任何企业，曾用‘工作完成’（Jobs to Be Done）的方法从零到一推出产品，并获得广泛采用？” 这就是他的挑战。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The latter, yeah, the product has done really well.
turns.zh: 在公司内部，还是说产品在市场上广泛采用？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: I already told you an example. I can't say it, but you can. The thing is, for example, Autobooks is another one that did this, right? They start to realize that the fact is you need to study the struggling moments and it helps you determine what not to build, right? Too many times we just keep adding more and more things to the product. And so in larger organizations it's very difficult because at some point the dominant market research is about hypothesis testing, "I'm going to go build a hypothesis and go basically then go build a research project to prove or disprove that hypothesis." (00:41:44): But the reality is, Jobs to Be Done research is hypothesis building research. I don't know, that's part of the point is we really don't know. We think we know, but Dr. Taguchi would always tell me there's way more unknown than there is known and never forget it. And so again, what causes people to buy windows is not what we think it is. And so you start to realize that. I think Drucker said it best, he goes, "What businesses think they're selling is not what customers are buying." And to be honest, he said that in 1953, and it's still true today. I just did interviews today where they're like, "Oh, people are buying for this reason," and we did 12 interviews and you started to realize, nope, that's not why they're buying. And they're shocked.
turns.zh: 我已经给过你一个例子了。我不能说出来，但你可以说。关键在于，例如，Autobooks就是这样做的，对吧？他们开始意识到，关键在于研究那些陷入困境的时刻，这能帮助你确定不该去开发什么功能。对吧？很多时候，我们只是不断给产品添加越来越多的功能。在大型组织中，这很难做到，因为在某个阶段，主流的市场研究都是围绕假设测试展开的：“我要去验证一个假设，然后再开展研究项目来证实或否定这个假设。” （00:41:44）但现实是，‘工作完成’研究本身就是假设构建研究。我不知道，关键就在于我们其实并不知道。我们自以为知道，但田口博士总是告诉我，未知远比已知多得多，不要忘记这一点。再说回来，促使人们购买窗户的原因，并不像我们想象的那样。我们开始意识到这一点。我认为德鲁克说得最贴切，他说：“企业以为自己在销售的东西，并非客户真正在购买。” 老实说，他在1953年就这么说了，但直到今天依然适用。我今天刚做完采访，他们会说：“哦，人们购买的原因是这个。” 我们做了12次采访，结果发现，不对，这不是他们购买的真正原因。他们都惊呆了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay, so you didn't say it, but maybe Facebook Marketplace?
turns.zh: 太棒了。好吧，所以你没说出来，但也许是Facebook Marketplace？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: So Autobooks would be one, you're trying from zero to one from nothing, right?
turns.zh: 所以Autobooks就是这样，从零到一，从无到有，对吧？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, brand new product is kind of the question there.
turns.zh: 是的，全新产品正是这个问题的核心。

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: Yeah, so at Techstars we basically make sure that everybody, they come in, they usually don't have a product to start with, at least in the Chicago and San Francisco offices. We basically have do jobs in the very, very beginning of that. And we have companies like Nutrisense and Havoc Shield, and there's a whole bunch of them that are out there that are growing and going down that pathway. And so to me, it's very, very useful, especially in the zero to one space. (00:43:08): But the notion is the way that I frame it is, what will people stop using when your product comes out? And that's who you want to go interview. So for the Marketplace thing, it was like, "Hey, I want them to stop using Craigslist. I want them to stop using eBay. I want them to stop using Etsy." If that's the case, what are they doing and how do I do it better than that so I can understand? There are really no new jobs, it's just the fact is we get better at them. And so the hire and fire criteria get better, but the context and outcome, most jobs, I can look back 10 years in the job existed and I can look ahead 20 years and the job's going to exist. It's just the nature of how the technology delivers on it is what gets better.
turns.zh: 是的，在Techstars，我们基本上确保每个人一开始都没有产品，至少在芝加哥和旧金山办公室是这样。我们在项目最初阶段就开展‘工作完成’研究。我们有像Nutrisense和Havoc Shield这样的公司，还有很多这样的公司正在成长并走上这条道路。对我来说，这非常非常有用，尤其是在从零到一的领域。（00:43:08）但我的理解方式是，当你的产品推出时，人们会停止使用什么？这就是你要去采访的人。比如Marketplace这件事，我们当时是这样想的：“嘿，我希望他们停止使用Craigslist，停止使用eBay，停止使用Etsy。” 如果是这样，他们现在在做什么，我该怎么做得比他们更好？没有真正的新工作，只是我们做得越来越好了。所以招聘和解雇的标准会提高，但大部分工作的背景和结果，我回看十年前这个工作存在，展望二十年后这个工作还会存在。这就是技术实现方式不断改进的本质。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. And it sounds like Intercom and Basecamp also are very early Jobs to Be Done adopters?
turns.zh: 太棒了。听起来Intercom和Basecamp也是很早采用"工作完成框架"（Jobs to Be Done）的公司？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: Very early, yeah.
turns.zh: 确实很早。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So I think with Sherom, something that I read between the lines is he worked at Twitter for many years and I think Twitter attempted at Jobs to Be Done framework, and I don't know if it went well and I think it just caused a lot of people to think this is a terrible framework.
turns.zh: 关于Sherom，我从字里行间读到，他在Twitter工作了很多年，而Twitter曾尝试过Jobs to Be Done框架，但我不知道结果如何，感觉这反而让很多人认为这个框架很糟糕。

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: This is where I think there's different flavors of it. And what I would say is that one flavor is really what I call very supply side driven, where it takes the underlying technology and then looks at it and says, "All right, what else can we do? Where can we be better? Where are things that are important but we're not satisfying on them?" And being able to prioritize. And so there's a very systematic approach that's hundreds of steps and very, very prescriptive in nature. (00:44:38): The method that I have and that I've been using mostly because I've been in the startup world and doing new to the world type stuff is it's very, very qualitative, organic, and it's a combination of a process, practice and skills. So every company actually has its own innovation process based on who they have, who they're serving, the underlying technology. And so, in my opinion, to have a very predictive one process that fits across everybody, I think there are principles, but I don't think there's one process. And so I think that's what they used at Twitter. (00:45:16): The other thing is that I think Jack was actually a big fan and he worked with Clay on a couple of things, but I don't think they worked on the method part of it, they worked on the thinking part of it. And so it was more about, so one of the most dangerous things you can do is sit in a room and hypothesize what the jobs are because I will guarantee you you're 100% wrong. And so this is what happens, by the way, this is the gift of dyslexia is I'm not an A student and so most A students don't start until they know the answer, most D students start because they don't know the answer. And so you start to realize we're wired very differently to do that. And so I always say that the A students have a disadvantage against the D students and entrepreneurship because we just go start and we learn right that in there. We don't have to hypothesize everything first because we actually don't know how to do that.
turns.zh:
我认为这个框架有不同的版本。我想说的是，其中一种版本非常偏向供应方导向，即先审视底层技术，然后问："我们还能做什么？哪里可以做得更好？哪些重要但尚未满足的需求？"并进行优先级排序。这是一个系统化的方法，包含数百个步骤，具有很强的规范性。
(00:44:38): 我使用的这个方法主要源于我在初创公司从事颠覆性创新工作，因此它非常注重定性分析、自然流畅，融合了流程、实践和技能。每个公司实际上都有基于自身团队、服务对象和底层技术的创新流程。在我看来，要想有一个适用于所有人的预测性流程，关键在于掌握其中的原则，而非单一的固定流程。Twitter当时采用的可能就是这种方法。
(00:45:16): 另外，我认为Jack曾是这个框架的忠实拥趸，他和Clay合作过一些项目，但我不确定他们是否深入研究了方法层面，而更多关注的是思维层面。最危险的做法就是坐在会议室里假设用户需求，因为我敢保证你100%会出错。顺便说一句，阅读障碍者的优势在于，我不是学霸，大多数学霸直到知道答案才开始行动，而差生则因为不知道答案而开始行动。因此我们会发现，我们的思维模式截然不同。我常说，学霸在创业中比差生处于劣势，因为我们直接行动，在实践中学习，而无需先假设一切。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So your advice there is essentially people often get Jobs to Be Done wrong because they just sit around and think about the Jobs to Be Done and aren't actually doing the work to interview and understand?
turns.zh: 所以你的建议是，人们常误解Jobs to Be Done框架，因为他们只是坐在那里假设用户需求，却不实际去做采访和理解工作？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: Yeah. They think more about the outcomes and they think about what's the best outcomes we can get for people. And what you start to realize is that there are trade-offs people make. And ultimately there's some irrational piece, some irrational component that makes everything twist around. The irrational component is like, why in the world do people eat Snickers when they're hungry? It's a candy bar. Well, it turns out when you bite it, it masticates into a ball and it sits in your stomach and it absorbs the acid that's causing you to say, "Hey, I got to eat something." And so part of it is the roll of the peanuts and the roll of the nougat is actually to masticate it together. The caramel should be sticking it together versus in a Milky Way, the melting temperature of the caramel is so light that you take a bite, it's liquid, you drink it down, you swallow it like it's a drink, it has nothing to do with food. (00:47:13): And so you start to realize that it's connecting the experiences to the context and outcome. It's connecting the supply side with the demand side, but it starts with the demand side first. Struggling moments and opportunities all exist before there's a product.
turns.zh:
是的。他们更多地考虑结果，思考如何为人们争取最佳成果。而你会逐渐意识到，人们会做出权衡取舍。最终，总会有一些非理性因素，让一切变得复杂。这种非理性因素就像，人们为什么会在饿的时候吃士力架？它毕竟只是一块糖果。结果发现，咬一口后，士力架会在口中咀嚼成一团，停留在胃里，刺激胃酸分泌，让人觉得“得吃点东西了”。因此，花生和牛轧糖的组合，实际上是为了将其更好地咀嚼融合。焦糖本应起黏合作用，但在士力架中，焦糖的融化温度极低——你咬一口是液态，吞下后像喝饮料一样，没有任何食物的感觉。（00:47:13）  
你会意识到，这是在将用户体验与上下文和结果相连接。它连接了供给端与需求端，但首先要从需求端入手。产品诞生前，必定存在痛苦时刻与机遇并存。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You're making me hungry.
turns.zh: 你让我饿了。

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: I bought a couple, but I didn't use them, but I bought a couple. And I mean, you go deep into it, you start to realize that this is the crazy part, everybody thinks they compete, but if you literally go back to a moment when you picked up a Snickers bar, you were not thinking about a Milky Way. You weren't thinking of half the candy aisle, you were thinking of like, "Do I want a sandwich, or do I want a Snickers?" Half the reason why they picked Snickers is it's 300 calories, I can eat it in three bites, it's done, it's not messy, and I can keep working. It's mainlining food.
turns.zh: 我买了几块，但没用完。不过我确实买了。深入探讨就会发现，这才是关键所在。所有人都以为在竞争，但若回溯到你拿起士力架的那一刻，你并没想起美味雪域（Milky Way）。你没有扫视一半糖果货架，而是思考：“我要吃三明治，还是士力架？”选择士力架的半个原因是它仅300卡路里，三口就能吃完，干净利落，还能继续工作。它是高效的能量补给。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I don't know if I've ever had a Milky Way to be honest.
turns.zh: 说实话，我好像从没吃过美味雪域。

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: That's right.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So I don't need that comfort.
turns.zh: 所以我不需要那种安慰。

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: That's the funny part is you go to all the big tech hubs in San Francisco and the Snickers are all empty and the Milky Ways are all full.
turns.zh: 有趣的是，你去旧金山那些科技中心，发现士力架都被吃光了，美味雪域却堆满了货架。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I get that. You mentioned that there's two different approaches or many different approaches to the Jobs to Be Done framework, and this is a question someone actually asked that there's maybe a framework by someone named Tony Ulwick, and then there's your approach, and then maybe Clay Christensen maybe has an approach. So can you just help clarify?
turns.zh: 是的，我明白了。你提到Jobs to Be Done框架有两种或多种不同的方法，有人提到的Tony Ulwick的框架，还有你的方法，Clay Christensen可能也有一套方法。能否帮我们理清一下？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: So Clay and I collaborated on it. So I was lucky enough to have Clay as a mentor for 27 years, I met with him once a quarter for 27 years, and at some point I shared with him the hack of how I was thinking about this and what I was doing, and at some point he said, "We need to turn it into a theory." To me, it was more like my work around because I couldn't read and write, "Let me go talk to some people, I'll figure it out." And ultimately we turned it into a method. So if you look at Competing Against Luck, it was written with Tady Hall and Karen Dillon, Dave Duncan, but I helped on that book for 16 months. Some of the clients in there are my clients. I think Intercom is in that one. So Clay and I are aligned in that. Clay was more about turning it to a theory and I would say I'm more about having it be a method. So his is like a thinking framework and a philosophy and a strategic kind of frame where mine is very tactical about how do we get it and then what do we do with it. (00:49:31): Ulwick's comes from a very different perspective, and again, I think it's very valuable, but it comes from the notion of functions and it's more like, what can our product do? What jobs can our product do? As opposed to the way I look at it is basically only people have jobs, products don't have jobs, people have jobs, organizations don't have jobs, people in organizations have jobs because that's the irrational part. And so fundamentally there's that two different views of how do we look at it, but ultimately I would say Clay's approach and my approach are derived from the same dataset where Ulwick's is derived from a different dataset and a different set of experiences.
turns.zh:
于是我和克莱一起合作完成了这项研究。能有克莱这样的导师相伴27年，我深感荣幸。27年间，我们每季度都会见面一次。在某个阶段，我向他分享了自己对此问题的思考和实践方法，他当时就说：“我们得把这套思路升华成一套理论。” 对我而言，这更像是临场应变——因为我当时既不会读也不会写，“先去和别人聊聊，再慢慢理出头绪”。最终我们将其转化为一套方法论。《与运气抗争》一书由我与塔迪·霍尔、凯伦·迪龙、戴夫·邓肯共同撰写，但我亲自参与了这本书16个月的创作，其中提到的部分客户正是我的客户。我记得Intercom就在书中被提及。克莱和我的观点存在共鸣——他更侧重于将其理论化，而我则更关注如何将其落地实践。

（00:49:31）乌尔维克的观点源自功能主义视角，我认为这也非常有价值，但其核心在于产品能做什么、能满足哪些需求。相较之下，我的观点基于一个基本前提：只有人有工作职责，产品没有工作职责，组织内的个人才有工作职责——因为这部分存在非理性因素。两者在方法论层面存在根本差异，但最终我认为克莱和我的方法论都源自相同的数据集，而乌尔维克的则基于不同数据集和经验体系。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's super interesting, I had no idea about this. And your sense is in the case of Twitter, for example, maybe it's closer to Clay's just think about it approach.
turns.zh: 这太有意思了，我之前完全不知道这些。就拿推特来说，或许它更接近克莱那种边想边做的方法。

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: Yep, I think that's right, I think that's right. And again, I think Ulwick's is very valuable, especially in some companies where there's lots of risk, there's regulation, there's lots of moving parts, very complicated systems, but at the same time it's so many steps. You have to have a very disciplined organization to follow it.
turns.zh: 没错，我觉得确实如此。乌尔维克的观点非常有价值，尤其适用于那些面临诸多风险、受监管、环节繁杂、系统复杂的公司，但同时也需要严密的组织架构来遵循这些规则。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: If someone wanted to start actually following through on this, which book would you recommend they start with to help them understand how to apply your approach?
turns.zh: 如果有人想实际践行这些方法，你会推荐从哪本书入手，让他们了解如何应用你的方法论？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: I would have them read Demand Side Sales, and it basically is starting from the theory of why do people buy and how do we actually understand how to flip the lens from trying to sell people things to help them buy? And ultimately it has the entire method around it kind of frame for product and for founders.
turns.zh: 我会推荐他们阅读《需求侧销售》。这本书从理论层面探讨人们为何购买，以及如何转换视角，从试图向人们推销产品转向帮助他们购买。最终它构建了一套完整的产品和创始人方法论框架。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Is Jobs to Be Done ever not the right framework for people to figure out what to build?
turns.zh: 太棒了。那《待完成的工作》是否永远不适合用来帮助人们确定要构建什么产品呢？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: Oh yeah. So couple places, one is when there's no choice or there's no real choice. So what's interesting is think about is why do you know more about your car insurance than your health insurance, right? And most of it is because your health insurance is given to you by your employer and you only utilize it when you're sick. But the car insurance, you have to pay for it so you have to sit down and decide what are the different trade-offs you're going to make where when you do it for the employer, it's good, better, best. And it literally is like, where am I my life? Have I been sick? There's some basic things, but there's no real choice there. (00:51:48): And so you start to realize where there's no real choice or where people want to make the choice obvious, it doesn't work. You have to be able to accept how people see you as opposed to how you want to be seen. So when companies will come to us and say, "All right, I want you to find these jobs for us," like, "Nope, I can't do it because it doesn't work. I can tell you what the demand side is asking for and then we can see how your product fits to it and what you have to modify to it, but if I try to help you build the case to make the jobs what you think they are, it doesn't work."
turns.zh: 是啊。有两种情况，一种是没有选择余地，或者说没有真正的选择机会。很有意思的是，你为什么对自己的汽车保险比对健康保险了解得多？主要是因为健康保险是雇主提供的，而且只有生病时才会用到。但汽车保险则需要自己花钱购买，所以你必须坐下来权衡各种取舍。当雇主提供保险时，人们往往觉得“好、更好、最好”。而现实中却是“我现在在哪儿？我生病过吗？” 有些基本问题是无法回避的，但缺乏真正的选择空间。（00:51:48）所以你会意识到，当人们没有真正的选择权，或者想把选择强加给别人时，往往行不通。你必须接受人们眼中的你，而不是你希望成为的自己。所以当公司来找我们说：“好吧，我想让你们帮我找到这些工作机会。” 我会说：“不行，我做不到，因为这行不通。我可以告诉你需求方在寻求什么，然后看看你的产品如何匹配，再做调整，但如果你试图帮他们把工作机会改造成你想象中的样子，那是行不通的。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: In those cases, is there a different framework you recommend or is it just like you don't really have a lot of options?
turns.zh: 在这些情况下，你有没有推荐的不同框架，还是说其实没太多选择？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: In a lot of cases to me, I'd do some ethnography, I'd literally figure out kind of where there's frictional points in the system. I might do some prototyping around kind of different alternatives, but typically it's more about what I would call the little hire or how do they use, for example, the health insurance as opposed to why do they buy the health insurance. (00:52:48): The other example I could use is chewing gum. If I talk to people about buying a pack of chewing gum, most people can't remember at all when they bought a pack of chewing gum, even if it was in the last week like, "Uh, I think so." But if I asked them when they chewed gum, they can tell me about when they chewed gum. And ultimately that will then imply when they buy gum. If you go to something that it doesn't register, it's so deep of a habit that they don't really know what they're doing, you'll never going to be able to get that information out of them. Again, the habitual stuff is very hard to see the job. It's only when people change do you see, it's like you can reveal the entire iceberg but if I've been using Tide for 20 years and I ask you why do you hire Tide, you just make it up. You have no idea why you Tide. But if you switch from Tide to Gain or Gain to Tide, you can tell me that story very detailed.
turns.zh: 对我来说，很多情况下我会做一些民族志研究，仔细找出系统中的摩擦点。可能会围绕不同的替代方案做一些原型设计，但通常更关注我所说的微观招聘，比如人们如何使用健康保险，而不是为什么购买健康保险。（00:52:48）另一个例子是口香糖。如果我问人们什么时候买了一包口香糖，大多数人根本记不清，哪怕是上周买的，也只能说“嗯，我想是吧”。但如果我问他们什么时候嚼口香糖，他们就能准确回忆起时间。这最终会揭示出购买口香糖的时间。面对一些不被注意的习惯，人们往往意识不到自己在做什么，你永远无法从他们那里获取这些信息。再说了，习惯性的行为很难被察觉。只有当人们改变习惯时，你才能看清全貌。就像你可以揭示整个冰山，但如果我用汰渍洗衣粉20年了，然后问你为什么用汰渍，你只能编造理由。你根本不知道自己为什么用汰渍。但如果你从汰渍换成佳能，或者从佳能换回汰渍，你就能详细描述整个过程。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's a reader who has the really interesting question, Maria Delano is her name. She's wondering, with a framework this well known, you're bound to get people misinterpreting it and repeating inaccurate information about the framework, and she's curious what misconceptions most frustrate you that you just hear again and again about Jobs to Be Done?
turns.zh: 有位读者提出了一个非常有趣的问题，她叫玛丽亚·德拉诺。她想知道，既然这个框架如此知名，难免会有人误解它，传播不准确的信息。她特别好奇，在“工作完成”框架方面，最让你感到沮丧的误解是什么？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: The first thing I want to say is actually, in doing it, I've explicitly made it very accessible because the moment you make it too copywritten, too patented, too whatever, people just move by it. So part of it was being able to make it in the public domain so people could have conversation and try it and do different things with it. (00:54:21): What I would say is there's enough people that have used it and have worked with it and have had great success with it that at some point in time, most of the people who are trying it and not using it well, it's obvious. And so it'd be lik, how do you double down into it? I think one of the biggest misconceptions around Jobs to Be Done is this notion that it's pain and gain as opposed to context and outcome. And that I think one of the other ones is it's purely about the outcome and not just about the context and outcome together. (00:54:51): And again, I think the biggest mistakes I've seen made is because they do it in a conference room and they don't go talk to people. They don't actually find the contradictions, they don't find the irrational parts. What's really interesting is when you hear somebody's story and it seems irrational, like we'll have people go, "Oh my God, that's an anomaly. That doesn't happen." But what you realize is that the context makes the irrational rational. So the moment you hear a story and you go, "I can't believe that," nine times out of 10 it's because you don't have the rest of the story. And so part of it's being able to understand the rest of that context that would drive somebody say, "Why would somebody cut their arm off?" Well, if they're in this situation and this and this and this, there's nobody who would say they want to cut their arm off, but in certain situations you'll do it. (00:55:37): And so that's what we're trying to do is find where will people change behavior? Most people are studying the momentum of where people are and what's the momentum of their direction, but the reality is what we're trying to do is study what causes people to change their direction. And that's where innovation happens. Innovation happens when people change.
turns.zh: 首先我想说的是，在实践过程中，我特意让这个框架尽可能易于理解，因为一旦它过于受版权、专利等限制，人们就会对它敬而远之。因此，我选择将其置于公共领域，让人们能够自由探讨、实践并进行各种创新。（00:54:21） 我想说的是，已经有足够多的人使用并实践了这个框架，并取得了巨大成功。到某个阶段，大多数没有用好它的人，其不足之处显而易见。那么，如何深化探索呢？我认为最大的误区在于，人们把Jobs to Be Done框架视为"痛苦与收益"的关系，而非"背景与结果"的关联。还有人误解为它只关注结果，而忽视了背景与结果的协同作用。（00:54:51） 再次强调，我见过最常见的错误是，人们在会议室里讨论，却不去实地调研。他们没有发现矛盾之处，也没有捕捉到不合理的细节。真正有趣的是，当你听别人讲述看似不合理的故事时，比如有人惊呼"天哪，这太反常了，这根本不可能"，但你会意识到，正是背景因素让不合理的行为变得合理。九成情况下，当你听到"难以置信"这样的反应时，往往是因为你没有了解完整的上下文。比如有人问"为什么有人会砍掉自己的手臂？"但如果了解完整的背景，你就会明白，在特定情境下，这种行为是可以理解的。（00:55:37） 因此，我们的核心工作是寻找人们行为转变的契机。大多数人研究的是人们当前所处的状态及其发展趋势，但我们真正关注的是推动人们改变方向的深层因素。创新正源于此——当人们改变方向时，创新才会发生。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What convinced you to spend your time and life working on Jobs to Be Done and helping people implement this framework and what keeps pulling you back?
turns.zh: 是什么促使你将时间和生命投入到Jobs to Be Done理论的实践中，帮助人们应用这个框架，又是什么力量持续吸引着你？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: That's a great question. So I think I started out as I just love to build things. My mom would take me, basically we have something around here called Big Trash Day is where they throw out the dishwasher and they throw out the old mini bike and all these different things. And my mom would basically say anything that we could fit in the trunk, we could bring home. And so I've been building things my whole life because I've been just always fascinated with how things work. So that's the first thing. (00:56:38): The second part is I love to help people. One of the things I realized is I can't build products for myself, and I've done seven startups, but I realized that I have to build for others. And so to me, building for others was where I started product. And then I realized that I'm a method builder and that I really help people innovate. And so I exist to help make the abstract concrete. So that phrase has helped lead me to becoming now a teacher and a professor and writing books is something I never wanted to do because I hated books. Clay convinced me that I had to learn how to speak and I had to write books. (00:57:18): So here's a really good one is that this is in 1990, so one of the things that happened was when my youngest kid moved out and basically moved out of the house, I had my notebooks from almost 30 years of every project on everything I worked on any company, and this is from one of my mentors, Dr. Taguchi, he said this in 1990 when I was living in Cologne, Germany. He said, "Write a book." So I opened this 30 years later, I'm like, "Oh, dang it. I got to write a book because he told me to." So it's just one of those things where I realized I really like helping people, I like creating methods. I'm very curious, sometimes annoyingly curious, but that's kind of the triad of things that I love to do.
turns.zh: 好问题。我觉得我最初只是喜欢动手做东西。我妈妈会带我去参加“大垃圾日”活动，当地会把洗碗机、旧迷你自行车之类的东西扔掉。我们基本上可以把能塞进后备箱的东西都带回家。所以我这辈子一直在做东西，因为我一直对事物的工作原理很着迷。这是第一个原因。（00:56:38）第二个原因是我喜欢帮助别人。后来我意识到，我没法只为自己开发产品，虽然我创办了七家初创公司，但最终我必须为他人服务。对我来说，为他人开发产品是产品开发的起点。我逐渐意识到自己是一个方法论构建者，能帮助人们创新。所以我的使命就是把抽象的东西具象化。这句话引导我成为了一名教师和教授，而写书是我从未想过要做的事，因为我讨厌书籍。但克莱说服我必须学会演讲和写作。（00:57:18）这里有个很有意思的故事。1990年，我最小的孩子搬出去住后，突然发现自己30年来积累的笔记本，记录了在每家公司参与的每个项目。这是我的导师田口博士在1990年德国科隆留学时对我说的话：“写本书吧。”30年后，我翻开这些笔记，突然意识到：“天哪，我必须写书了，因为他让我这么做的。”这就是我意识到自己喜欢帮助别人、创造方法论的时刻。我好奇心很强，有时甚至让人觉得烦，但这三件事正是我的热爱所在。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Bob, is there anything else you wanted to share or touch on or make sure we cover before we get to our very exciting lightning round?
turns.zh: 太棒了。鲍勃，在进入激动人心的闪电问答环节之前，你还有什么想分享、探讨或确保我们涵盖的内容吗？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: There's three big things to take away. One is struggling moments is the key and it's struggling moments that people take action on. And what I would say is they're everywhere. They are freaking everywhere in our lives and there's only certain contexts when all of a sudden we realize we have to do something about it. So study struggling moments because at some point that's where we need the innovation the most. The second thing is think about the progress people are trying to make. What is their standard, not your standard? What is that context? What is that outcome? And the last thing, the way I phrase it is choose what to suck at and figure out the trade-offs that you need to make and make sure that your trade-offs map the trade-offs of the customer. Because nine times out of 10, most products that fail is because they made a trade-off that the customer didn't agree with.
turns.zh: 有三个关键要点需要提炼。第一，困境时刻是关键，人们往往在困境时刻采取行动。这些时刻无处不在，充斥着我们的生活，但只有在特定情境下，我们才会突然意识到必须采取行动。因此，研究困境时刻至关重要，因为这正是我们最需要创新的时刻。第二，思考人们试图达成的进步目标。他们的标准是什么？背景是什么？结果又是什么？最后，用我常说的话来说，选择你不擅长的领域，权衡取舍，确保你的取舍与客户的取舍相契合。因为90%失败的产品，都是因为做出了客户无法认同的取舍。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Well, with that, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. I've got six questions for you. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的，接下来是激动人心的闪电问答环节。我有六个问题要问你。你准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: Yeah, I'm ready. Always ready for these.
turns.zh: 好的，我准备好了。随时待命。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Perfect. What are two or three books that you've recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 完美。你推荐给别人最多的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: Shape Up by Ryan Singer, it's phenomenal. The other book I would say is End of Average by Todd Rose. I listen to it every single year. I get something on it every single year. I've been listening to it for probably eight or 10 years. I literally called Todd, I've become friends with Todd. We interact on a regular basis. It's an amazing book.
turns.zh: 瑞安·辛格（Ryan Singer）的《塑造自我》（Shape Up），这本书太棒了。另一本我要推荐的是托德·罗斯（Todd Rose）的《终结平均》（End of Average）。我每年都会听一遍，每次都能从中收获新启发。我听这本书大概有八到十年了。我甚至直接给托德打过电话，我们现在成了好朋友，经常交流。这本书真是太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What is a favorite recent movie or TV show?
turns.zh: 最近有没有喜欢的电影或电视剧？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: I love Big Bang. I watch it every... People would say that I'm Sheldon, I think I'm more Leonard, but I can see there's days that I come across as Sheldon, I don't mean to be Sheldon. But I like Oppenheimer. I think any of the science type, I'm not really a science fiction person, but it's more about, I'll say historic documentaries, I love them all because they help me understand the science.
turns.zh: 我超爱《生活大爆炸》（Big Bang）。我每周都看……人们说我像谢尔顿（Sheldon），但我觉得自己更像莱纳德（Leonard）。不过有时候也会表现得像谢尔顿，我又不是故意的。但我很喜欢《奥本海默》（Oppenheimer）。我对科学题材的作品很感兴趣，虽然我不算科幻迷，但我更喜欢历史纪录片，因为它们能帮助我理解科学原理。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What is a favorite interview question you like to ask when you're interviewing people?
turns.zh: 面试别人时，你最喜欢问的三个问题是什么？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: What are the top three things you struggle with in your business today that if you could solve would fundamentally change the business?
turns.zh: 目前你的业务中最头疼的三个问题是什么？如果能解决其中一个，业务会发生根本性改变？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Love it. What is a favorite product you recently discovered that you just really like?
turns.zh: 太喜欢了。最近有没有发现特别喜欢的产品？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: I recently purchased a massage chair, and it's one of those things where I've been getting massages for a while, and as I get older and I'm working out more, I've lost almost 100 pounds. And so I'm to the point where I'm working out more and God, nobody told me I'm going to be cold all the time, I'm sore all the time and I'm hungry all the time. And so it's like, "Okay, I need a way in which this..." So I would get a massage every two weeks or so, and now I can get a massage in 20 minutes on demand. And it's pretty freaking amazing.
turns.zh: 我最近买了一台按摩椅。我以前一直去按摩店按摩，但随着年龄增长，锻炼越来越多，我体重减了快100磅。现在我更常自己按摩，但天啊，没人告诉我会一直觉得冷、浑身酸痛、老是饿。这时候我就想：“好吧，我需要个解决办法……”以前每两周去按摩一次，现在随时都能按摩，简直太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Man, my wife has wanted one of these and this might be good for her.
turns.zh: 哇，我妻子也一直想买这个，或许对她也有用。

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: Oh, I will tell you, it's a life changer. It is one of those things where we'll do interviews and I can go do an interview and a debrief, pop in and do it. And I'm brush as I can be. It's better than an app.
turns.zh: 哦，我跟你说，这真是改变了我的生活。每次采访前，我们可以先做采访和汇报，直接进入状态。我现在随便刷刷手机就行了。比用app好多了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there a brand you want to throw out that you found to be your favorite?
turns.zh: 有没有你特别喜欢的品牌？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: Kyoto is the one that I have.
turns.zh: 京都茶道。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Kyoto.
turns.zh: 京都茶道。

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: I got it from Costco. It's fabulous.
turns.zh: 我在好市多（Costco）买的。太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, we'll be looking into that. What is something relatively minor you've changed in how a company has implemented Jobs to Be Done that has had a big impact on their ability to do it well?
turns.zh: 好的，我们会调查一下的。在公司实施“工作完成理论”（Jobs to Be Done）时，有没有什么相对细微的调整，却对做好这项工作产生了重大影响？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: There's two. One is Intercom. So the way that Intercom really took off and why it did so well is actually, it was Des Traynor and Eoghan McCabe who were the two founders, they actually studied, they came to one of my workshops in the beginning, but they studied it and they tried to do it, and then we talked about it. But then they brought Matt Hodges and Paul Adams and Sean Townson and the executive team, and they did the interviews. And when they did the interviews, they understood what to do and it literally all went downhill from there. And they knew how to ask the questions.
turns.zh: 有两个例子。第一个是Intercom。Intercom之所以能成功，关键在于创始人德斯·特雷诺（Des Traynor）和伊奥汉·麦凯布（Eoghan McCabe），他们认真研究了这个理论，刚开始参加了我的研讨会，但后来自己实践。他们带着马特·霍奇斯（Matt Hodges）、保罗·亚当斯（Paul Adams）、肖恩·汤森（Sean Townson）和整个管理团队一起做访谈。通过访谈，他们彻底理解了方法，之后一切都顺风顺水了。他们很清楚该怎么提问。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Downhill in a good way?
turns.zh: 以一种积极的方式迎接挑战？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: They knew how to do the interviews way. It was kind of amazing. And Paul Adams and Matt Hodge's first day at Intercom was in my office in Detroit. So that to me is one of the key. (01:02:23): The other is to find a place in a very large organization where a group is struggling, they can't deliver product, they can't move fast enough, they keep getting the wrong insights, they say it's going to be this big, and literally focusing on a very small area and giving them a little space to demonstrate the use of it, and then it will spread with a case study or two. And so most companies, if they start small case studies and sharing it with people both when it works and not works, or starting with the top.
turns.zh: 他们知道如何高效地进行采访。这真是令人惊叹。保罗·亚当斯和马特·霍奇在Intercom的首日工作是在我位于底特律的办公室进行的。对我而言，这就是关键所在。（01:02:23）另一个关键点是，在大型组织中找到一个正在苦苦挣扎的团队——他们无法交付产品、无法快速推进项目、不断得出错误的洞察、声称项目会大获成功，却始终未能实现。于是，我们专注于一个极小的领域，为他们留出空间展示其应用效果，随后借助一两个成功案例让理念得以推广。大多数公司若想启动小型案例研究并与他人分享成果，无论成功与否，都需从高层着手。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Two more questions, one is, someone asked me to ask you the dining room table story. Does that ring any sort of bell?
turns.zh: 再问两个问题：有人让我向你讲述餐桌故事。这能让你想起什么吗？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: Yeah. So one of the things I did is I built houses. So before I built houses, I was running a venture capital, private equity firm. We had about 100 million. I was doing 25 transactions and just traveling too much, I had four children. And so my wife and I kind of had the conversation that I wound it down and I said, "What am I going to do?" I wanted to try and find a business I could work in and be part of and own part of so I joined a building company here in Detroit, and we ended up building a thousand homes here in Detroit and had 14 sites. And one of the things we did is we built for downsizers like your parents. And one of the things they constantly told us was, "Look, we're downsizing. We're not having the holidays. We're done with that. I don't want a dining room table, so we can't even have people over. If we're going to do it, we're going to go somewhere else. I don't want the dining room table." (01:03:50): And so we made, it's a two bedroom, two and a half bath, first floor laundry, gourmet kitchen, kind of amazing condo. But what we realized is people, if they didn't know where the dining room table was going to go, they weren't going to move. And so it turns out that the dining table was the emotional bank account for their entire life. And so if you weren't going to take it or your sister wasn't going to take it or your brother wasn't going to take it, the reality is they weren't going to give it the Goodwill, it was not going to go in the basement. It might go into the storage unit, but for the most part, people would literally stay where they are until they knew where the dining table's going to go. (01:04:25): So I did the opposite of what they told me to do, which is I built a place to put the dining room table. You could never eat at it, it was never big enough to actually pull the chairs out of it, but it was still a symbolic of what it was and they would use it for puzzles and that kind of stuff. But I sacrificed the second bedroom suite to basically add that, and it increased sales 22%. So this is a case where you learn, again, that irrational contradiction that says, "They've said this, but you did that. That doesn't make any sense." That's what jobs helps you with, those kinds of really important, small but subtle and important insights.
turns.zh: 是的。我曾从事房地产业务。在此之前，我经营着一家风险投资和私募股权公司，管理着约1亿美元的资金，完成了25笔交易，但旅行频繁，身为四个孩子的父亲，我与妻子决定放慢脚步。于是，我加入了底特律一家建筑公司，最终在底特律建造了1000套住宅，开发了14个项目。其中一项业务是为像你父母那样的下层阶级家庭建造住宅。他们不断强调：“看，我们在缩小居住空间，不再过节，不再需要餐桌。我们不需要餐桌，所以不能邀请客人。如果要用餐，我们会去别的地方。”（01:03:50）于是我们打造了两卧两卫、一楼设洗衣房、配有美食厨房的精品公寓。但我们发现，人们若不知道餐桌该放在哪里，便寸步不让。原来，餐桌承载着他们整个生活的情感记忆。若你不搬走它，姐妹不接手，兄弟不继承，现实就是不会把它捐给慈善机构，也不会藏进地下室，可能会放进仓储间。但大多数人会原地等待，直到确定餐桌的安置位置。（01:04:25）我反其道而行之，专门建造了一个放置餐桌的空间。虽然没法在上面用餐，椅子也拉不出来，却象征着餐桌的存在。他们会用它来拼拼图之类的。我牺牲了次卧套房来增设这个空间，最终销售额提升了22%。这个案例再次告诉我们，人们常说：“他们这么说，但你却反其道行之。”这正是工作教会你的东西——那些看似矛盾却至关重要的小而巧妙的洞察力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Last question, you showed me this very cool camera setup you have in one of the views was your heroes on the wall?
turns.zh: 最后一个问题，你向我展示了办公室里很酷的摄像头设置，墙上挂着你的偶像？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: Yeah, yeah, yeah.
turns.zh: 是的，是的，是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Can you show that and share who those folks are?
turns.zh: 能把这些人介绍一下吗？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: Yeah, so at the end of the night, I have this philosophy that I have the energy in your body and your brain literally you need to use every ounce of it every day because you wake up the next day with a full bank account and you can't really save it. So every night I paint. And so these are paintings of my mentors and they're above me, but Dr. Deming, Clay, Dr. Taguchi, and Dr. Willie Moore, I wrote about him in a book called Learning to Build, and the five skills that they taught me to enable me to kind of work on so many different things in different areas. (01:05:45): And so Deming I met when I was 18, he took me to Japan. I worked for Ford and I was responsible on the front lines to help reduce product development cycle time at Ford from 72 months to 36 months. So that's where I learned a lot of tools and methods and things like that from Toyota. And then I learned Dr. Taguchi's method, which is amazing around designed experiments. Dr. Willie Moore was my first boss at Ford, and she was a PhD in particle physics and she taught me empathetic perspective of how to see things and frame things and really amazing, amazing individual. (01:06:20): And then the last one was Clay Christensen, which is I just walked in his office and he had a sign outside his office basically saying anomalies wanted, and I walked in and I said, "Look, I'm an anomaly. I don't really know if you want anomalies, but I am." And we sat down and started talking, and ultimately I asked him, "What's your research and how can I help?" He had been there maybe about a year, and it was one of those things where he got kind of somber and it was almost like he had a tear, and I was like, "What's going on?" He goes, "I've been here a year and everybody's asked me for things, but nobody's ever asked to help me, and you're the first person." And so that was the beginning of the relationship, and I had four hours a quarter for 27 years with Clay with no agenda, which is kind of amazing.
turns.zh:
好的，我每晚结束工作后，都有个理念：你体内和大脑里的能量必须被充分利用，因为第二天醒来时银行账户的余额就归零了。所以每晚我都会画画。这些画像是我的导师，他们都在我上方——田中一郎博士、克莱·克里斯滕森、田口彰二博士和威利·摩尔博士。我在《学会建造》一书中写过威利·摩尔，他教会了我五项技能，让我能在不同领域开展工作。（01:05:45）：我18岁时结识了田中一郎博士，他带我去日本。我当时在福特工作，负责缩短产品开发周期，从72个月缩短到36个月。这段经历让我从丰田学到许多工具和方法。接着我掌握了田口彰二博士的实验设计法。威利·摩尔博士是我在福特的第一位上司，她拥有粒子物理学博士学位，教会我以同理心看待事物、构建框架，真是个了不起的人。
（01:06:20）：最后一位是克莱·克里斯滕森。我走进他的办公室时，门外挂着招募"异常现象"的牌子。我说：“看，我就是个异常现象。不知道你是否需要，但我就是。”我们坐下来交谈，最后我问：“你的研究内容是什么，我能如何帮忙？”他刚到那里约一年。当时他神情凝重，几乎眼含泪水，我问：“怎么了？”他说：“我来一年了，所有人都向我索取，却没人想帮我，你是第一个。”这就是我们关系的开端。27年来，我每季度与克莱共度四小时交流，没有任何议程安排，真是难得。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's incredible. What a beautiful way to wrap up our chat, Bob. My job to be done for this interview was to help people understand Jobs to Be Done. I think we accomplished our goal as much as we can in one hour. Two final questions, where can folks find you online if they want to reach out and maybe ask you a question?
turns.zh: 太不可思议了。鲍勃，这真是结束我们对话的绝佳方式。我这次采访的任务是帮助人们理解"待完成工作"理论。我觉得我们在一小时内尽可能达成了目标。最后两个问题：如果读者想联系你或提问，可以在哪里找到你？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: Yeah, LinkedIn is probably the best place, and I post most of the stuff there. And then I have several different companies, but one is called The Rewired Group, and I've had that for about 14 years, and that's a design consultancy agency around helping people build and launch products. And we do everything from Fortune 100 to not-for-profits, to startups and different ways. And then I have something called Laser Ventures where we actually work for equity and we also put money into investments as well. And that's called Laser Ventures with Andrew Glazer. And we have a podcast called The Circuit Breaker, which it's more or less all these different concepts in 20 minute format of me and my partner just riffing around what is the empathetic perspective or what are the forces of progress? Or just small little things that basically help people learn along the way, and it's just long enough for a commute or a walk or something like that.
turns.zh: 是的，领英是最佳平台，我大部分内容都在那里发布。我还有几家公司，其中一家叫The Rewired Group，经营了约14年，是一家设计咨询机构，专注于帮助人们开发和推出产品。服务对象从《财富》100强企业到非营利组织，再到初创企业，业务形式多样。还有Laser Ventures，我们以股权形式投资项目。这是与安德鲁·格雷泽合作的项目。我们还运营播客《The Circuit Breaker》，通过20分钟的形式探讨各种概念，比如同理心视角、进步的驱动力，以及能帮助人们学习的点滴智慧，时长刚好适合通勤或散步等场景。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Last question, how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 最后一个问题：听众如何能为你提供帮助？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: To be honest, I was so excited for this podcast. I was excited, one, because I'm a fan, but two is to see your post and then get all those responses. I think I said, "Boy, I think we need more than an hour. This is amazing." And so to be honest, posting questions, asking questions, letting the community kind of interact. And what was so interesting is it was people who had questions, but then there were people like Des and Jason who reached out and said, "Oh, this will be awesome. You'll love this." All those kind things. (01:08:51): So to me, just keep being a community. And what I would say is, as this is posted, just put more questions up there. The hard part for me is actually answering questions in a written form. My request would be is that if we can figure out a format so I can answer them more in a conversation where we almost like a list of things where there might be a follow-up of some sort, but if your listeners could literally help me by being more articulate, that would be great.
turns.zh: 老实说，我对这期播客特别兴奋。一方面是因为我本身就是粉丝，另一方面是看到你们的帖子后收到了那么多回复。我当时就感叹：“天哪，我觉得我们需要超过一小时的时间来聊这个，太棒了！”说实话，发布问题，征集回答，让社区互动起来，真的很有意思。有的人有问题要问，但也有像德斯和杰森这样主动联系我们的人，他们说：“哦，这一定会很棒的。你会喜欢的。”大家都这么热情。（01:08:51）所以对我来说，继续保持社区的活力很重要。我想说，当这个帖子发布后，大家可以多提些问题。对我来说，用文字回答问题比较难。我希望能找到一种更便捷的形式，让我能更像是在对话中回答问题——比如列个清单，再做些后续补充，但如果听众能更清晰地表达想法，帮我把问题翻译得更准确，那就太好了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Let's figure out if we can do some way of doing that, that would be amazing.
turns.zh: 好的，我们看看能不能找到合适的办法实现这个想法，那就太棒了。

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: That would be great.
turns.zh: 那真是太好了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Bob, again, thank you so much for being here.
turns.zh: 鲍勃，再次感谢你能来。

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: Thanks. Thanks for having me.
turns.zh: 谢谢。感谢邀请我。
